name: Ashmark Patchlayer Thermal Liner Vest
description: A salvage-constructed quilted liner vest stitched from mismatched fabric scraps — old military surplus, transit upholstery, reclaimed insulated panels — all in muted earth tones that somehow cohere. Worn under a coat or over a shirt, it adds a full thermal zone without bulk. No brand markings; the stitching itself is the signature.
functionality: Layered salvage insulation for core warmth; no-bulk profile for under-coat or standalone wear.
what_it_says: You make do, and you've made do well enough that it almost looks deliberate.
manufacturer: Ashmark Street Construct — no fixed maker
story_hooks: One of the fabric panels is cut from a corporate uniform — the logo has been removed but the weave pattern is unmistakably Stratum Logistics.
The vest has been repaired so many times the original stitching is impossible to identify — it's effectively a different garment than it started as.

physical_description.visual_profile: A visibly patchwork quilted vest with an understated, utilitarian silhouette. The mismatched fabric blocks create an organic, almost topographic texture across the torso. Worn loose enough to layer comfortably, it reads as functional street wear—the kind of thing that's been assembled from necessity rather than design.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed, unstructured fit designed for layering. Sits at the natural waist with enough room to wear over a shirt or under an outer coat. Arm holes are wide and unstretched, suggesting modular construction rather than tailored geometry.
physical_description.primary_material: Salvaged composite: reclaimed military twill, transit upholstery fabric, weathered canvas sections, and heat-reflective insulation panels stitched together. All mid-lifecycle materials—worn in but still structurally sound.
physical_description.texture: Heavily quilted in irregular patterns, each patch showing distinct weave and nap. Some sections are smooth ballistic weave, others rougher canvas or knit-backed upholstery. The stitching itself is visible, irregular, and sometimes doubled or reinforced.
physical_description.color_scheme: Muted earth palette: charcoal, sage green, rust brown, weathered tan, and deep olive. No color blocked deliberately—instead a naturalistic patchwork where adjacent scraps are close enough in tone to read as cohesive from distance.
physical_description.closures: None—pulls on over the head. The construction is simple enough that no fastening is needed; it functions as a compression layer.
distinctive_features: Visibly hand-stitched or hand-repaired seams with varying thread colors and stitch density
Thermal insulation panels integrated asymmetrically where salvage allowed
Possible faint stenciling or fading marks from original garment purposes (military insignia, transit route numbers) still visible beneath patches
No tags, labels, or maker's mark—only the stitch pattern itself serves as proof of origin
Weight and bulk distribution uneven due to insulation placement
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 salvage. This is post-consumer rework, the uniform of the ungoverned zones and waste-management crews.
physical_description.cultural_context: Wearing this signals bootstrap resourcefulness, street economy participation, or active rejection of corpo supply chains. Common among waste workers, independent couriers, and sub-grade residential communities. It's honest wear—no pretense, no false scarcity markup.
physical_description.condition_typical: Worn and weathered from first day of use. Seams show stress, edges are soft from handling, and the patchwork develops its own wear patterns as thermal zones compress differently.

Vest layered over a plain dark undershirt, photographed against an industrial concrete wall with sickly green neon ambient light casting long shadows. Shallow depth of field isolates the irregular quilting and stitching patterns. Grainy, documentary-style capture emphasizing material authenticity and salvage origins. Moody, low-key lighting.
